To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) leaf litter leaching is an important source of metals for aquatic ecosystems and (2) contaminated leaf litter leaching might have small additional toxic effects on aquatic consumers.

i) metal concentrations in leaf litter are higher in polluted than in uncontaminated areas; ii) metal release from leaf litter is high and is mainly due to the release of potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus; iii) leachate toxicity is mainly due to phenolic compounds, but metal release from leaf litters collected from polluted sites is slightly more toxic than from uncontaminated ones.

the release of metals from leaf litter during leaching may represent a source of pollution in adjacent ecosystems and that the leachates of contaminated leaf litter are slightly toxic for a detritivorous species, Gammarus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential risks of metal release from leaf litter and leaching toxicity for aquatic food webs.
the fate of metals from contaminated leaf litter, and the potential toxicity of the resulting leachates for aquatic organisms.
the potential risks associated to the dispersion of leaf litter from polluted sites in aquatic ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the release of leaf litter from polluted sites into aquatic environments might not be the most important pathway of metal dispersion from polluted sites to aquatic ecosystems.

the dispersion of leaf litter from contaminated sites in adjacent ecosystems might represent a potential source of pollution for aquatic ecosystems, but that the associated risks are probably limited.

contaminated leaf litter is a potential source of pollution for aquatic ecosystems, especially for detritivorous species, which may have important ecological consequences for the structure and functioning of these ecosystems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the release of metal-contaminated leaf litter leachate in the environment might not be a major source of metal contamination in aquatic ecosystems but might be a source of phenolic compounds, which are known to be toxic to aquatic organisms.

, in the context of a contaminated soil, the use of uncontaminated leaf litters in ecotoxicology studies would be a good option to avoid potential confounding effects of leaf litter leachate toxicity, but the use of contaminated litters could be an interesting alternative to study the potential chronic effects of leaf litter contamination on aquatic ecosystems.

the dispersion of leaf litter in aquatic ecosystems is not negligible and might represent a non-trivial source of pollution, especially for metal-polluted sites, but that its effects on aquatic organisms are probably limited to a short-term exposure to leaf litter leaching.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dispersion of leaf litter from polluted soils may be a non-neglected source of contaminants in aquatic ecosystems.
the use of uncontaminated leaf litters in ecotoxicological experiments should be avoided, as it may induce an underestimation of toxic effects of contaminated leaf litters on organisms.

, in order to evaluate the risks associated with metal-contaminated leaf litter dispersion, the use of toxicity tests with leaf litter leachate is more appropriate than direct exposure of test organisms to leaf litter.
